content: Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is not effective against chloroquine-resistant strains of Plasmodium falciparum. Children are particularly sensitive to 4-aminoquinoline compounds, and even small doses (e.g., 0.75 g or 1 g) can be fatal in a 3-year-old child. Patients must be strongly advised to keep this medication out of the reach of children to prevent accidental ingestion. The use of hydroxychloroquine sulfate in patients with psoriasis may trigger a severe exacerbation of the condition. Similarly, in patients with porphyria, the drug may worsen the disease. Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should not be used in these conditions unless, in the physician's judgment, the potential benefits to the patient outweigh the possible risks. During pregnancy, the use of hydroxychloroquine sulfate should generally be avoided unless it is being used for the suppression or treatment of malaria, and only if the physician determines that the benefits outweigh the potential hazards. It is important to note that studies involving intravenously administered radiolabeled chloroquine in pregnant, pigmented CBA mice demonstrated that the drug crosses the placenta rapidly. It selectively accumulates in the melanin-containing structures of the fetal eyes and remains in the ocular tissues for up to five months after the drug has been eliminated from the rest of the body. Antimalarial compounds, including hydroxychloroquine sulfate, should be used with caution in patients with hepatic disease, alcoholism, or when used concurrently with other known hepatotoxic drugs. For patients undergoing prolonged therapy, periodic blood cell counts should be performed. If a severe blood disorder develops that cannot be attributed to the underlying disease being treated, discontinuation of the drug should be considered. Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should also be administered with caution in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, as these individuals may be at increased risk for hemolysis.
